kurz: How rebalancing brings a portfolio back to its originally chosen allocation and why this almost always costs return.

bloecke.md:
A portfolio that was once set to a ratio of 70 to 30 does not keep this allocation. Its components grow at different speeds. Because equities rise more strongly over the long term than bonds or instant-access savings, the mix always shifts in the same direction, towards more risk. Rebalancing reverses this shift. This involves selling what has risen and buying what has lagged behind.

Rebalancing is often presented as a way of earning more return. Its primary purpose, however, is to control risk.

## Drift in the equity allocation

The shift in the mix, known as **drift**, is considerable. A portfolio of 60% US equities and 40% ten-year US government bonds that was set up at the end of 1989 and never changed afterwards consisted of 91.5% equities at the end of 2025. Calculated over the full 98 years from 1928 to 2025, the equity allocation rose to 99.6%, so the bond portion practically disappeared.

More important than the final level is when the deviation occurs. At the end of 1999, immediately before the technology bubble burst, the equity allocation was 79.5%; at the end of 2007, shortly before the financial crisis, it was 71.9%. Drift is therefore greatest after long good periods. If a slump then follows, it hits the portfolio at a time when its equity allocation is particularly high.

bloecke.titel: Equity allocation of a 60/40 portfolio, 1990 to 2025
bloecke.unter: Without rebalancing, the equity allocation rises from 60% to 91.5%; the setbacks of 2002 and 2008 only lower it temporarily.

bloecke.md:
## Costs and benefits

Four variants are compared using the same data over 36 years. The portfolio reset annually trails the one that is never adjusted by 0.57 percentage points a year, but in return its fluctuation is around two points lower. In the long series from 1928 to 2025, the gap is larger, at 8.34% versus 9.45% a year. The return forgone there is 1.11 percentage points.

This is because rebalancing systematically sells whatever has recently performed better. If one asset class performs better than the other for decades, this is a disadvantage. If the class in the lead changes, it is an advantage. In the period from 2000 to 2025, which includes the so-called lost decade for equities, the sign reversed. There the rebalanced portfolio came out ahead, at 6.94% versus 6.77%.

On risk, the result is clearer. The largest decline on a year-end basis was 18.0% for the rebalanced portfolio (in 2022, when equities and bonds fell together) and 21.2% for the never-adjusted one, up to the end of 2002. The larger loss arose because this portfolio went into the crash with almost 80% in equities.

bloecke.titel: 60/40 in US equities and ten-year government bonds, 1990 to 2025

bloecke.unter: The three 60/40 variants lie almost on one line, along which lower volatility goes hand in hand with lower return; rebalancing shifts the position along this line but does not improve the ratio of return to volatility.

bloecke.md: Rebalancing is a decision about risk and not about return. Investors who practise it for the sake of a higher return are disappointed in long equity bull markets. They then usually give it up at the point when the equity allocation is furthest above its target.

## Bernstein's rebalancing premium

Under certain conditions, rebalancing produces additional return, but only within narrow limits. In 1996, William Bernstein tested an approximation formula for this effect on 105 pairs of assets. It explained the measured premiums with a coefficient of determination of 0.983, that is, almost completely.

No returns appear in the formula. It gives the lead of the rebalanced portfolio over the weighted average of the two individual returns and can never become negative. This lead only amounts to a gain over a never-adjusted portfolio if both assets deliver roughly the same return over the long term. In that case, repeated reallocation pays off, because rebalancing converts fluctuations into return. If the returns diverge significantly, the opposing effect, that is, shifting money into the weaker class, predominates, and the rebalanced portfolio falls behind the never-adjusted one. For a US portfolio of 50% each in equities and long-term corporate bonds, Bernstein measured a premium of 0.49 percentage points a year over the weighted average for the years 1926 to 1994 (8.34% instead of 7.85%). The never-adjusted portfolio achieved 9.17% over the same period. As in the 36 years of the table above, the opposing effect therefore predominated.

bloecke.formel: RB = w1 × w2 × [ sd1 × sd2 × (1 - rho) + (sd1 - sd2)² / 2 ]
bloecke.erklaerung: Approximation of the rebalancing premium according to Bernstein (1996). The premium rises the lower the correlation, the higher the fluctuations and the more the two levels of fluctuation differ.
variablen: target weights of the two assets
correlation coefficient of the two assets
additional return per year, as a decimal
bloecke.beispiel: 50/50 mix of equities (sd 0.18) and bonds (sd 0.06) with rho = 0.1 and assuming equal returns: RB = 0.25 × [0.18 × 0.06 × 0.9 + 0.12² / 2] = 0.25 × 0.01692 = 0.0042, so around 0.42 percentage points a year.

bloecke.md:
## Calendar or tolerance band

Two sets of rules are in common use. With the **calendar**, the portfolio is rebalanced on a fixed date, for example every January or on your birthday. With the **tolerance band**, action depends on a deviation, regardless of the date.

On frequency, the evidence is clear. Vanguard concludes that monthly or quarterly rebalancing improves neither risk nor return compared with annual rebalancing and only increases turnover. Larry Swedroe's widely used **5/25 rule** provides for rebalancing when a main asset class deviates from its target by 5 percentage points in absolute terms or a smaller position by 25% in relative terms. With a 70% target allocation, the band therefore runs from 65% to 75%. For a 5% position, the relative threshold is triggered at 3.75% and 6.25% respectively. In 2008, Gobind Daryanani found a relative band of around 20% to be a favourable value. According to his results, it is sufficient to check every ten trading days.

In the simulation above, the band does just as well as the calendar but needs only a third of the transactions. This is its most important advantage, and it carries particular weight in Germany.

A band rule can be checked often and is still rarely executed. Under a strict calendar rule, by contrast, the portfolio is rebalanced even for a deviation of 0.8 percentage points. This incurs costs and taxes without noticeably changing the risk.

## Rebalancing through inflows

As long as you are still saving, rebalancing can do without sales in most years. Ongoing savings contributions, dividends and interest go entirely into the underweight class until the target allocation is reached again. This incurs no tax and often no order fee either, and no decision has to be made in a crash.

The target allocation is 70/30 and the portfolio value €50,000 (€35,000 in equities, €15,000 in bonds). A year later, the equities have risen by 25% to €43,750 and the bonds by 1% to €15,150. The portfolio is now worth €58,900, and the equity allocation is 74.3%.

Route 1 is selling. Target equity value = 0.70 × 58,900 = €41,230. Equity holdings worth €2,520 have to be sold, and the money goes straight into the bond portion. The allocation is right on the same day, but flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) is due.

Route 2 is buying more. The equity portion stays at €43,750. For this to be 70%, the portfolio has to grow to 43,750 / 0.70 = €62,500. That requires €3,600 of new money, all of it for the bond portion. With monthly savings of €500, this takes just over seven months, and no tax is incurred.

Route 2 needs more capital and more time; route 1 costs more tax. Until the portfolio is much larger than the amount saved each year, route 2 is almost always preferable.

## Tax consequences in Germany

Every sale in a private securities account realises gains and thus triggers [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax]]. It amounts to 25% plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on top, 26.375% in total, or just under 28% with church tax. For equity funds and equity ETFs, 30% of the income remains tax-free through the [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act). In a larger portfolio, the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (€2,000 for joint assessment) is usually already used up by distributions and the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale).

As a worked example, take a sale of equity ETF units for €8,000 in which 40% of the proceeds is price gain. That gives a gain of €3,200, of which 30% is exempt. This leaves a tax base of €2,240 and tax of €590.80, which is 7.4% of the amount reallocated. The order fee, by contrast, ranges from zero to a low double-digit amount, depending on the provider. The bid-ask spread of large world ETFs on Xetra is around two to four basis points, so less than four euros here. Tax is therefore by far the largest cost item; the other costs hardly matter.

However, reallocating only makes the tax fall due earlier, because the units will be sold at some point anyway. It is therefore a matter of **bringing tax forward** and not an additional tax. The disadvantage is the lost compound interest on the amount paid earlier. If the €590.80 stayed invested for another 20 years at 6%, it would grow to around €1,895. The increase of around €1,300 would also be taxable on the later sale. After tax, the loss from the forgone deferral therefore comes to about €1,060 per €8,000 reallocated.

bloecke.md: Under Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG (Income Tax Act), for securities held in collective safe custody, the units acquired first are deemed to be sold first (FIFO principle). Investors who have been saving monthly for ten years therefore sell their oldest units when rebalancing, and these are the ones with the highest share of gains. The tax burden is therefore regularly higher than the average gain share of the portfolio would suggest. Within the same securities account, you cannot choose which units are sold.

- Set a fixed band in writing, for example 5 percentage points for the main asset classes, and check it once a quarter.
- Correct deviations first through savings contributions, dividends and interest. Only sell if this cannot close the gap within a year.
- Where reallocation is tax-neutral, act there first, for example in an insurance wrapper, a Rürup or Riester contract or an occupational pension.
- Direct new purchases into a second securities account. This keeps old and new units separate and lets you control the FIFO order.
- Stick to the date after crashes. Buying more when prices are falling is the only unpleasant part of the process and at the same time the only part that restores the risk allocation.

The rule does not take into account whether the underweight class has fallen for good reason. Under it, you keep buying more as long as money is available. Japanese equities did not exceed their peak of 29 December 1989 again until 22 February 2024. A rebalancing rule would therefore have spent 34 years buying into a market that did not regain its old level.

The procedure nevertheless remains sensible if the order is right. First the target allocation is reviewed, then the portfolio is rebalanced. Rebalancing restores a decision that has been made but does not review it. It only protects against the risk of a single market if the target allocation itself is diversified broadly enough. Even a globally diversified equity portion, however, consisted of 40% to 45% Japan at the end of 1989 (weight in the MSCI World). With weighting by market value, this share then fell along with prices, without any targeted additional buying.

Rebalancing is countercyclical, because it sells winners and buys losers. A momentum strategy does the opposite, and there is robust evidence for it too. The contradiction is resolved by the different time frames. Momentum is measured over months, mean reversion over years. Whether rebalancing dates should therefore be postponed has not been reliably established. The measured differences between annual and quarterly rebalancing are small anyway compared with the tax effect.

mitnehmen: Without intervention, the equity allocation of a 60/40 portfolio rises to over 90% in 36 years, and it rises most strongly shortly before each slump.
Rebalancing keeps risk constant and in exchange usually costs return, 0.6 to 1.1 percentage points a year in the long US series.
An advantage over a never-adjusted portfolio only arises if both classes have similar returns, low correlation and high fluctuations; if the returns diverge significantly, the effect is negative.
Annual rebalancing is sufficient, and bands such as 5 percentage points absolute or 25% relative achieve the same with a third of the transactions.
In Germany, flat-rate withholding tax is the largest cost item when reallocating, and rebalancing through new savings contributions avoids it completely.

begriffe.text: Resetting a portfolio to its target allocation by selling overweight components and buying underweight ones. It keeps risk constant but does not maximise return.

Reallocating only once a set deviation has been exceeded, instead of on fixed dates. The 5/25 rule is widely used, with thresholds of 5 percentage points absolute or 25% relative to the target weight.

Additional return over the weighted average of the individual returns that arises from systematic reallocation. According to Bernstein, it is never negative and is greatest with low correlation and high fluctuation. Compared with a never-adjusted portfolio, rebalancing only has the advantage when returns are similar.
Restoring the target allocation solely by directing new savings contributions, dividends and interest into the underweight class. In Germany, this does not trigger flat-rate withholding tax.

Under Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG, for securities held in collective safe custody, the units bought first are deemed to be sold first. When rebalancing, this means that the oldest units with the highest gains are realised.
